facts.fact: Depth Anything V2 Small runs at 60 ms with 25M parameters and reports 95.3% DA-2K accuracy (paper's own table, as summarized in search results).
Depth Anything V2 DA-2K accuracy is 89.8% when trained on labeled synthetic data alone and 95.3% with pseudo-labeled real data alone (per search-result summary of the paper).
Depth Anything V2 ViT-L reaches NYU-D delta1 0.984 and AbsRel 0.056 (per search-result summary of the paper's table).
No search result reported a face-specific accuracy evaluation of Depth Anything V2; its benchmarks are general scenes.

Depth Anything V2 is described as a relative-depth model (ordering of near/far) that does not recover absolute metric distance; this is a secondary characterization from search snippets, not checked against the paper text.

In one autonomous-vehicle obstacle-avoidance study, Depth Anything V2 showed the highest accuracy among compared monocular methods, with low and stable error across distances (study-specific setup; numbers not retrieved).
A robotics assessment concluded Depth Anything V2 gives higher pixel resolution than LiDAR but significantly reduced metric depth accuracy.
In a drone photogrammetry study with low-overlap aerial images, both monocular networks showed meter-level errors; MiDaS v3.1 had notably higher errors than Depth Anything v2.
Marigold (CVPR 2024, Ke et al.) repurposes a diffusion image generator (Stable Diffusion) as an affine-invariant monocular depth estimator.
The extended Marigold paper (arXiv 2505.09358) adds Marigold-Normals, a surface-normal variant following the Marigold-Depth fine-tuning protocol.
Marigold V2 (arXiv 2609.08084) replaces the Stable Diffusion backbone with a diffusion transformer (Qwen-Image-Edit per search summary) and the authors claim state-of-the-art surface normals results.
The Marigold V2 repo includes a normals configuration that uses an angular loss.
DSINE uses per-pixel ray direction and learns the relative rotation between neighboring surface normals; code is public.
DSINE is reported as trained on about 160K images and surpassing Omnidata-V2 trained on over 12M images (attribution in snippet is unclear; treat as secondary).
DSINE scores a mean angular error of about 16.4 degrees on NYUv2 as cited in other papers (arXiv 2607.12450 and the Lotus benchmark table).
A 2026 paper, Face Normal Estimation from Rags to Riches (arXiv 2601.01950), proposes exemplar-based refinement of a coarse face normal; the snippet does not show whether DSINE is a baseline.
A 2020 paper (arXiv 2003.09691) estimates face normals from in-the-wild images using cross-modal deep face normals with deactivable skip connections.
Sapiens is a Meta human-centric vision model family covering pose, body-part segmentation, depth and surface normals, pretrained on over 300 million in-the-wild human images.
Sapiens depth and normal training used synthetic data generated from 600 detailed RenderPeople scans (per search summary).

Sapiens reports 22.4% relative RMSE improvement on Hi4D (depth) and 53.5% relative angular error improvement on THuman2 (normal) over prior work (as summarized in search results; baseline details not verified).
A later paper describes Sapiens fine-tuning on 500K high-resolution synthetic images for depth and normal estimation.
Depth Anything 3 (arXiv 2511.10647) was reported as published November 14, 2025 by a community ComfyUI wrapper; no official announcement was checked.
The official DA3 repo offers a DA3Metric-Large model; metric depth is computed as focal x net output / 300, where focal is the mean of fx and fy.
DA3-metric is reported with best SUN-RGBD AbsRel of 0.105 and second-best on DIODE (per search summary of the paper).
DA3Metric-Large is listed at roughly 350M parameters by community wrappers.
An official-looking community TensorRT ROS2 node exists for DA3 monocular metric depth, indicating GPU/TensorRT deployment paths; no CPU latency was retrieved.

contradictions: Depth Anything V2 is praised as most accurate in an autonomous-vehicle study but found to have significantly reduced metric accuracy in a robotics LiDAR comparison; the setups differ, so both should be reported.
DSINE's training-data-efficiency claim (160K vs 12M images) comes from a secondary snippet with unclear attribution.
